steps.en: Artefacts are false images the machine draws when sound misbehaves: echoes that arrive late, beams that stray sideways, and signals that wrap past their limit. Every artefact has a fingerprint and a fix, and the examiner expects both. The dangerous errors run two ways: calling an artefact real, such as a reverberation posing as a mass, and calling real disease an artefact, such as dismissing a small vegetation as side lobe fuzz. Learn each fingerprint with its confirming manoeuvre.
Suspect artefact whenever a structure repeats at doubled depth, crosses anatomy it should not, or vanishes with a small probe move.
Test reverberation by spotting equally spaced parallel lines from a strong reflector such as calcium or a catheter.
Test shadowing by tracing the dark band behind calcium, prostheses or ribs back to its bright source.
Test side lobe by watching the fuzz beside a bright curved reflector change as you angle the probe.
Test mirror image by confirming the duplicate sits beyond a strong reflector such as the diaphragm at matched distance.
Test refraction and range ambiguity with a second window before believing odd positions or duplicate traces.
Calling near field reverberation a thrombus or mass. Fix: Slide off axis and rescan. A true mass persists in two windows; reverberation does not.
Reading dropout behind rib shadow as a wall defect. Fix: Angle around the rib or ask for a breath hold. The hidden wall reappears when the beam clears the bone.
Grading colour mosaic as severe regurgitation. Fix: Raise the scale and confirm with spectral Doppler. Aliasing is physics, not turbulence severity.
Accepting a foreshortened apex as the true apex. Fix: Slide apically until the cavity lengthens. A short rounded apex also overreads ejection fraction.
Reverberation fingerprint. Equally spaced parallel echoes at multiples of the reflector depth. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on imaging artefacts
Shadowing rule. Strong reflectors block sound; nothing behind them can be judged. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on imaging artefacts
Mirror image rule. Duplicate appears beyond a strong reflector at matched distance. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on imaging artefacts
Aliasing rule. Signal wraps past the Nyquist limit, half the pulse repetition frequency. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination, section on Doppler artefacts
Side lobe fuzz inside a chamber mimics smoke or thrombus until you angle the probe and watch it move.
Refraction at tissue boundaries duplicates or displaces structures, so confirm odd positions in two windows.
A true mass persists across windows and probes while artefacts shift, which is the single best discriminator.

remember.en: Confirm odd structures in two windows before believing them

q.en: Equally spaced parallel lines behind a calcified valve are what?

why.en: Reverberation bounces between the probe and a strong reflector, painting equally spaced repeats at multiples of its depth.

q.en: A dense shadow hides the far wall. What follows?

o.en: Nothing behind it can be judged

why.en: Shadow means no sound reached the far field, so any wall down there cannot be judged until another window clears the reflector.

q.en: A suspected thrombus appears only in one window near a bright reflector. What next?

o.en: Angle the probe and rescan in a second window
Raise the gain to burn through

why.en: True masses persist across windows while artefacts shift or vanish, so a second window is the discriminator.
